newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia trying to subvert Chechen poll - Maskhadov.
newsitem.headline: Russia trying to subvert Chechen poll - Maskhadov.

text.p: Chechen presidential candidate Aslan Maskhadov on Monday accused Russia of trying to sabotage the breakaway region's elections and said any cancellation of the polls would threaten the peace process.

"In Russia everything possible is being done to prevent the elections taking place. This is the reason for the anti-Chechen hysteria in Russia and the return of the image of the Chechen bandit," Maskhadov told Reuters in an interview.

He said recent comments by Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and other Russian politicians insisting Chechnya stay within the Russian Federation had been designed to "destabilise the situation" in the region on the eve of voting.
Maskhadov, chief commander of the Chechen rebel fighters during their 21-month battle against Russian troops, is one of the front-runners in the January 27 presidential election.

"Somebody still needs a war but we in Chechnya have nothing left to lose, nothing left to burn or destroy," said Maskhadov, who was also the rebels' main negotiator in peace talks with Moscow that finally brought a halt to hostilities last August.
At his home outside the Chechen capital Grozny, the clean-shaven, mildly-spoken Maskhadov, wearing a leather jacket and traditional lambswool hat, said the elections must go ahead as planned.
"Cancelling them would freeze the peace process for a long time, which is precisely what the opponents of Chechen independence want," he said.

Maskhadov and other rebel leaders believe that some Russian politicians and sections of the media are exaggerating the instability in post-war Chechnya in a bid to sully the region's image and to discredit its fledgling democracy.

Some rebels have suggested that rogue elements within the Russian secret services were involved in a rash of criminal incidents in Chechnya, including the murder last month of six foreign relief workers by unidentified gunmen.

The incident triggered the withdrawal of all international aid organisations from the war-ravaged region. It also fuelled doubts that Chechnya's interim rebel government would be able to guarantee the safety of international election monitors or of foreign journalists during the election campaign.
Moscow called the shooting a tragic criminal act which should not stop the elections taking place.

The peace deal with Moscow, signed on August 31, effectively defers a decision on Chechnya's final status for five years but the rebels regard this as just a face-saving form of words for Russia following its military defeat.
Maskhadov, generally seen in Moscow as a man it can do business with, said Russia had nothing to fear from the elections and said he would seek friendly relations if elected.

"After the elections we must immediately decide around the negotiating table what kind of relations we will have with Russia," he said, adding that Chechnya wanted to be protected by international laws and guarantees from future aggression.
If elected, he said another top priority would be tackling a post-war crime wave sweeping Chechnya.
"Chechens, Russians, foreigners -- all must be free to walk our streets without fear," he said.
On a typically defiant note, Maskhadov said: "Our land is rich, we don't need to beg for anything from Russia."

"We don't expect anything from the West (either) because it closed its eyes to the genocide that Russia launched against the Chechen people. We long ago reached the conclusion that only Allah will help us," he said.
